summary:
Haryāna stands under the national framework of India. No Haryāna-specific trans-related statute, enforcement series or incident pattern with a source was identified, so the state is scored at the national position and a visitor's expectations are set by central law.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, amending the 2019 Act, and it awaits presidential assent. The bill ends the self-identification route to legal recognition established by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment in NALSA v Union of India, confines recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and otherwise recognises only male and female categories. Trans men, trans women and people who self-identify as gender-fluid or non-binary fall outside the recognition scheme.

Medical certification becomes a condition of recognition. The amendment mandates certification by a medical board and a district authority before gender-affirming surgery, and conditions identity recognition on medical procedure. For a trans visitor whose papers rest on self-declaration, that shift bears directly on how documents are read at entry, at police contact and at any administrative counter in Haryāna.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these provisions echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the bill as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics counter that the narrower definition excludes a large share of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
Parliament's passage of the bill on 25 March 2026 was met with protests in Mumbai, indicating organised opposition and public contestation around recognition rather than a settled transition.

The 2026 amendment reverses the direction set by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling and narrows the 2019 Act rather than expanding it, so the operative trend in Indian recognition law is contraction of who qualifies, not broadening.

Civil-liberties and rights organisations, including the People's Union for Civil Liberties and activists such as Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as an attack on the right to exist, framing the measure as criminalising in effect even where it is drafted as a welfare and anti-trafficking instrument.
localsOnly:
Residents of Haryāna seeking legal recognition of gender must meet the categories the amended central Act allows: historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex persons, with male or female as the only other recognised markers. Self-identification alone no longer suffices once the amendment is assented to.

Gender-affirming surgery requires certification by a medical board and a district authority under the amended scheme, which places a clinical and administrative gate in front of medical care that the 2019 Act did not impose in this form.

The new 'coercing or alluring' offences expose residents to prosecution, and the People's Union for Civil Liberties has warned that the provisions reproduce the logic of colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people.

Access to welfare schemes is the benefit the government cites for the amendment; whether Haryāna's state departments have issued implementing instructions for those schemes is not sourced here.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill is recorded as pending in the sources; whether it has since been granted, and on what date, is unresolved in this inventory.

No Haryāna-specific source on police conduct, checkpoint practice, detention conditions or documented incidents involving trans people was available for this record, so state-level enforcement remains not sourced rather than assessed as absent.

Whether Haryāna state authorities have issued circulars, training directives or facility rules implementing the amended central Act is not sourced and should be verified before relying on it.
